question: List five (5) military achievements of Joshua the Son of Nun.
idealAnswer: The book of Joshua deals with the conquest and settlement of the Promised Land after the death of Moses, and at every step Joshua was successful. His military achievements include the invasion of the land (chapters 1–5) and the crossing of the River Jordan; the capture and fall of Jericho (chapter 6); the conquest of the south (chapter 10); the conquest of the north (chapters 11–12); and the quick military operations against the important cities of Canaan, which all illustrate his successes. To these may be added the division of the conquered land among the tribes and the appointment of cities of refuge (chapters 13–22). His one failure was at Ai, because Achan coveted some of the spoils from Jericho.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Analysis of the Book of Amos
question: Describe the Vision of the Basket of the Summer Fruit in Amos 8:1-14. Outline the activities of the cruel and materialistic merchants of the Northern Kingdom and the result after the judgments.
idealAnswer: In the fourth of Amos' five visions of doom the Lord showed the prophet a basket filled with ripe summer fruit, and then explained to him that it symbolised Israel, which was now ripe for judgment. The vision is directed against the cruel and materialistic merchants of the Northern Kingdom, whose activities Amos sets out. They robbed the poor by selling them mouldy food and trampled upon the needy. They longed for the Sabbath to end and for the various religious holidays to be over, so that they might once again start cheating, using their weighted scales and undersized measures. And they made slaves of the poor, buying them for a debt of a piece of silver or for a pair of shoes. Amos then declares the results that would follow when this judgment took place: the sound of singing in the Temple would be turned to weeping; dead bodies would be scattered everywhere; fearful heavenly signs would occur (8:9); and there would be no comforting words from God (8:11-12). The vision thus belongs with the other visions – the locusts, the fire, the plumb line and the Lord at the altar – in which Amos declares that God would no longer turn away from punishing his people.

subject: OT

question: Amos ends his prophecy on a positive note concerning the future restoration of Israel. List any four of these areas and explain how this is going to happen.
idealAnswer: Amos ends his prophecy on a positive note concerning the future restoration of Israel, and five areas of restoration are named. The first is the restoration of the Davidic dynasty (9:11a). God had made a covenant with David that there would always be a descendant to sit on his throne, and though the exile made that promise seem impossible, “in that day” God would raise up and restore the kingdom to its promised glory – a promise fulfilled not by an earthly political leader but by the promised Messiah, who would renew the spiritual Kingdom and reign for ever. The second is the restoration of unity in the nation (9:11b-12). The kingdom had been divided in 931 B.C. in the reign of Rehoboam, and Amos declares that the fallen tent will be rebuilt as it used to be, referring to a restored united kingdom: “I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel”. The third is the restoration of agriculture (9:13). The soil will be so fertile that the reaper will be overtaken by the ploughman and the planter by the one treading grapes, so that seedtime and harvest follow in rapid succession without interruption by drought or plague, and new wine will drip from the mountains and flow from all the hills. The fourth is the restoration of the people (9:14a): during the exile the Jews would be scattered all over the world, and this promise refers to the bringing back of the captives from everywhere they had been scattered. The fifth is the restoration of liberty (9:14b): they will plant vineyards and gardens and will eat their crop and drink their wine, being in control of their own produce instead of growing crops as tribute for other nations. Amos adds that this restoration would be permanent (9:15): “I will plant Israel in their own land, never again to be uprooted from the land I have given them.”

question: Although Amos was from the Southern Kingdom – Judah, he was commissioned by God to preach in the Northern Kingdom city of Bethel. Historically describe Bethel.
idealAnswer: Bethel was historically one of the places where significant events had taken place in the life of Israel. Abraham had encamped there (Genesis 12:8). It was there that Jacob had his famous dream (Genesis 28:10-22), and the dream so moved him that he gave the place the name “Bethel”, which means “House of God”; before that the place had been known as Luz (Genesis 28:19). The history of the town changed when the United Kingdom was divided in 931 B.C. (1 Kings 12). Bethel then became one of the two major religious sites of the Northern Kingdom, and it was there that the idolatrous worship of the golden calf was instituted, a worship that continued to the end of the Northern Kingdom. Thus Bethel, the house of God, became the house of iniquity. It was about this place that Amos prophesied (Amos 7:10-13), and it was to Bethel that God commissioned him, a man of Judah, to go and preach.

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: What is divorce? How does God view divorce according to Malachi chapter two?
idealAnswer: Divorce, as Malachi 2:14-16 presents it, is the putting away of a wife – and not merely the putting away of a woman, but the putting away of a woman who is a man's companion and the wife of his covenant. In Malachi's day the men of Israel were marrying pagan women who were idolaters, which God had expressly forbidden, and were making the offence worse by divorcing the Jewish wives of their youth: the older men were cruelly divorcing their ageing wives and marrying attractive young foreigners, so that family life suffered. God views divorce in four ways. First, it is an act of cruelty (2:14), because the woman put away is “his companion”, one who has shared her life and life's experiences with her husband, and he writes her off as if it were nothing; that is cruelty and callousness. Secondly, it is an act of disloyalty (2:14), because she is not only his companion but “the wife of thy covenant”: he vowed his life to her, left father and mother to cleave to his wife and vowed never to let her go, but his vow has turned out to be empty words. Thirdly, it is an act which frustrates God's design of a godly seed (2:15): when a man divorces the wife of his youth and gets involved in a mixed marriage the future of the children is placed in jeopardy, for it is only when parents remain faithful to their marriage vows that God's desire for godly children will be fulfilled. Fourthly, it is an act which God hates: “I HATE DIVORCE” (2:16). God hates evil, and his children are to have the same attitude toward it, as Paul says, “abhor what is evil” (Romans 12:9). Divorce therefore shows a failure of the faithfulness God requires of his people, faithfulness to himself and faithfulness in human relationships.

subject: OT

question: The church has intensified her teaching on tithe, and you have been called upon to give a teaching on tithing in your society as a lay preacher. Write down your thoughts on the topic.
idealAnswer: The Hebrew word for tithe is ma'aser, and it means a “tenth”. Its origin is difficult to trace, but it is known to have existed in ancient Babylon and also in Persia, Egypt and China, and it is quite certain that Abraham knew of it when he migrated from Ur, for he gave a tenth to Melchizedek, priest of the Most High, so that in Abraham's day the giving of tithes had already been recognised as a holy deed. When Jacob made his covenant with God at Bethel the payment of tithe was included (Genesis 28:16-22). The legal requirement of tithing developed late and customs varied. At first the one who paid the tithe was entitled to share it with the Levites (Deuteronomy 14:22-23); after the Levitical code was completed the tithes belonged exclusively to the Levites (Numbers 18:21), who in turn gave a tenth of what they received to provide for the priests (Numbers 18:25-32). A Hebrew who lived too far from the temple could sell his animals and buy substitutes at the temple with the money (Deuteronomy 14:24-26), a permission which eventually led to gross abuses by the priests, which our Lord rebuked when he cleansed the temple. Leviticus 27:30 makes it clear that a tithe of everything belongs to the Lord and is holy to the Lord, and Deuteronomy 12:5-12 instructs that the tithe is to be brought to the house of God, not partaken of at home, while each Hebrew had to make a declaration of honesty before the Lord so that no deceit would be practised (Deuteronomy 26:13-15). Tithing was thus God's way in Old Testament days of providing the means to sustain his work and to provide for his ministers, the priests. In Malachi's day there had been a total disregard for this rule: the people disobeyed the clear instructions of God's word and were therefore robbing God, being greedy and self-centred in spite of God's goodness to them, and they were now experiencing God's chastisement and being deprived of his blessing (Malachi 3:7-9). What should they do? The answer is simple: they must repent and “bring the whole tithe into the storehouse”. If they are willing to do this, God will open the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing on them, and will also remove the chastisement they were experiencing in their agriculture (Malachi 3:10-12). It is believed that by the time of Jesus this injunction was being obeyed, so that teaching on it was hardly necessary; in Matthew 23:23 and Luke 11:42 Jesus encouraged his hearers to continue to pay their tithes but to be mindful also of the weightier matters of the law – justice, mercy and faithfulness. That is the balance our own teaching on tithing must keep.
keyPoints: The Hebrew word for tithe is ma'aser, meaning a tenth
Tithing was known in Babylon, Persia, Egypt and China, and Abraham knew of it (Genesis 14; Hebrews 7:4)
Jacob included the payment of tithe in his covenant with God at Bethel (Genesis 28:16-22)
At first the tithe was shared with the Levites (Deuteronomy 14:22-23); later it belonged exclusively to them (Numbers 18:21)
The Levites gave a tenth of the tithe to provide for the priests (Numbers 18:25-32)
A tithe of everything belongs to the Lord and is holy to the Lord (Leviticus 27:30)
The tithe is to be brought to the house of God (Deuteronomy 12:5-12), with a declaration of honesty (Deuteronomy 26:13-15)
Tithing sustains God's work and provides for his ministers
In Malachi's day the people robbed God and were deprived of his blessing (Malachi 3:7-9)
They must repent and bring the whole tithe into the storehouse; God will open the windows of heaven (Malachi 3:10-12)
Jesus urged the payment of tithes together with justice, mercy and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23; Luke 11:42)

subject: OT
topic: The Ministry of Malachi
question: In discussing the date for the Ministry of Malachi, it is argued that he worked after the return from the Babylonian Exile. Give five reasons to either support or refute this claim by Bible scholars.
idealAnswer: The exact time of Malachi's ministry is not given in the book, but several indications place it after the return from the Babylonian Exile, in the period of Ezra and Nehemiah. First, the prophet mentions a “governor” as being over the land (1:8); this was the political condition that existed when the Jews returned from Babylon, whereas before the exile the political leader of the nation was a king, and Haggai likewise used the word governor of Zerubbabel. Secondly, he must have prophesied after the ministry of Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied during the building of the temple (520–516 B.C.), for there is no reference in Malachi to the rebuilding of the temple. Thirdly, the impression of a drift into a casual attitude towards worship shows that some time had passed since the rebuilding: the temple services had been resumed long enough for the priests to become weary with the regular performance of them (1:13), and irregularities had crept in (1:7-8, 12-14; 3:8-9). Fourthly, there are details which link the prophet to the time of Nehemiah, especially the latter years of his governorship over Judah; Nehemiah came to Jerusalem as governor in 445 B.C., served some years and returned temporarily to Persia in 433 B.C. Fifthly, on his return to Jerusalem Nehemiah found gross sin and violation of the Law (Nehemiah 13), and there is a very close agreement between Nehemiah 13 and the book of Malachi, from which we may infer that Malachi prophesied during the return of Nehemiah, probably a few years after 433 B.C. The claim of the scholars is therefore to be supported: Malachi is a post-exilic prophet, indeed the last prophet of the Old Testament, after whom came the four hundred years of silence.

He mentions a “governor” over the land (1:8) – a post-exilic condition; before the exile the leader was a king
Haggai used the word governor of Zerubbabel
He prophesied after Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied during the temple building (520–516 B.C.)
There is no reference to the rebuilding of the temple
Temple services had been resumed long enough for the priests to grow weary and for irregularities to creep in
Details link him to the time of Nehemiah, especially the latter years of his governorship
Nehemiah came as governor in 445 B.C. and returned to Persia in 433 B.C.
The close agreement between Nehemiah 13 and Malachi suggests he prophesied a few years after 433 B.C.

subject: OT
topic: Brief Survey of the Former Prophets
question: Write a brief introduction to the book of Judges and, using the prophetic interpretation of the pattern of history, give the five stages of the analysis of the book.
idealAnswer: Judges covers the period in Israel's history between Joshua's death and the rise of Samuel, roughly 1220 to 1050 B.C. It was a time of transition in which the only thing that held the scattered tribes together was their common faith: loyalty to God meant a strong united nation, while turning to the gods around brought weakness and division. The story in Judges chapter 1 gives the impression that Israel under Joshua could not drive out the Canaanites as the book of Joshua portrays, and this failure leads on to a story of increasing chaos and confusion; one thing that comes out clearly is that history continually repeated itself through the period, a pattern of failure repeated later in Samuel and Kings. The prophetic interpretation of this pattern is described carefully in Judges 2:11-23, in five stages. First, the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the Lord; they forsook the Lord and served the Baals, the gods of the Canaanites. Secondly, the Lord's anger came upon Israel and he gave them up into the hands of foreign powers – the Moabites, Midianites, Amorites and Philistines. Thirdly, they cried to the Lord, and he had pity on his people's sufferings and raised up judges to deliver them, among them Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, Abimelech, Tola, Jair and Jephthah. Fourthly, the judges were given military victory and success by God against their enemies. Fifthly, when the judges died the people returned to their old sinful and idolatrous ways, and so the pattern of failure started all over again. The book ends with an appendix (chapters 17–21) illustrating the moral and religious decline of those times, and the explanation given for the state of affairs is that “there was no king in Israel and every man did what was right in his own eyes” (Judges 17:6; 21:25).

The appendix (17–21) shows the moral decline: there was no king in Israel

subject: OT
chapter: INTRODUCTION TO PROPHETS AND PROPHECY IN ISRAEL
topic: Facts about Prophecy in Israel
question: Write a note on any two of the following: a. The role of the Prophets in Israel. b. The prophetic Word. c. The Prophetic Action. d. Prophecy and the Future.
idealAnswer:
a. The role of the prophets in Israel. The prophets played a variety of roles in the life of Israel. They gave oracles, which was generally consultative; they preached and taught during worship; they interceded on behalf of the people, as Amos prayed that the judgment of God should not come upon his people, and they also spoke of the needs of the people to God; and they declared the will and the purpose of God even when this was not requested and in other contexts than the cultic services. Their ministry was unpredictable, for the prophet was free to act as and when the Spirit of God directed. They were feared in society and free from all constraints, so that Jeremiah, who would otherwise have been persecuted as a traitor after his first utterance, had the sovereign freedom to say what he was directed to say, as Nathan did to David (2 Samuel 12:1-12).

b. The prophetic Word. In ancient Israel the WORD was something very important. A man's spoken word had great significance, and the written word was not as important as the spoken word, since few could read and write. It was your spoken word that testified against you in court; the blessing was a powerful word, and when Jacob stole the blessing it could not be taken back, so that when Esau asked “what is left for me?” his father answered “nothing”. The word had an independent power and was an instrument of effective power. That is why the word of the prophet was very important; and the prophetic word was the very word of God, not the prophet's own words, and the same word was to be proclaimed by the prophet.

c. The Prophetic Action. The prophets do not only speak but act, and this is what is termed the prophetic action or prophetic symbolism. The prophetic action is itself creative of what it depicts: Ezekiel, for example, builds a city on sand with mud and makes a toy soldier (Ezekiel 4), by which he meant that he was helping to bring about the siege and destruction of Jerusalem. These actions were not just illustrations but depicted what was likely to happen, and the performing of the action was in itself a contribution to bringing about what was conveyed, for the prophetic actions were believed to contain power to shape the future.

d. Prophecy and the Future. A commonly held meaning of the word prophecy is “to predict the future”, but that is not its proper meaning. In the Old Testament the word means to speak the word of God. Prophecy therefore takes many forms: sometimes it is an explanation of past events, sometimes a warning, an admonition or appeal, a piece of advice or exhortation in the present, and sometimes it is directed to the future. Prophecy in the Old Testament has a past reference occasionally, a future reference occasionally and the present most often, for the prophets were primarily religious commentators on the life they saw around them, including its social, economic and political life. Very often the future reference was to the immediate future and was conditional – “if you do not repent, then …” – though the writing prophets also foretold the certainty of God's future plans and occasionally referred to the coming of Christ.
keyPoints: Roles: giving oracles (consultative); preaching and teaching during worship; interceding for the people; declaring God's will unasked
The prophets were free and unpredictable, feared in society, e.g. Nathan and David
The spoken word had great significance in Israel and was more important than the written word
The word had independent power; the prophetic word was the very word of God, not the prophet's own
Prophetic action or symbolism: the prophets act as well as speak, e.g. Ezekiel's city of mud (Ezekiel 4)
Prophetic actions were not mere illustrations but were believed to contain power to shape the future
Prophecy does not properly mean to predict the future but to speak the word of God
Prophecy has a past reference occasionally, a future reference occasionally and the present most often
Future references were often to the immediate future and conditional on repentance

subject: OT
topic: Outline of the Book of Malachi
question: Discuss this statement in the view of Malachi 3:13-4:6: “It is vain to serve God; and what profit is there to serve God?”
idealAnswer: This complaint belongs to the last of the six charges of the book, that Israel had discredited God's service. The majority of the people said that it does not pay to serve the Lord (3:13-15). They complained that they were religious, that they had kept the law of God and his charge and had walked in mourning before him, but that it had not been profitable to them and God had not rewarded them; God, they said, let the “real sinners” get away with their sin and even blessed them. In reality the statement was untrue, and the ones who complained were themselves the ungodly sinners: although they were religious and went through the motions of religious rites, it was superficial and external, they were hypocrites and had no heart for God, and their arrogant complaining was a discrediting of God's service. Over against them stood the remnant or minority in the nation, who believed that it does pay to serve the Lord (3:16-4:3). Among those who profess to know God there is always a remnant who truly are godly; though blessing may be delayed they do not complain, but wait patiently for him. Three things are said about the godly: they feared or reverenced the Lord and served him faithfully; they spoke to one another, defending God's actions and exhorting one another not to lose heart in spite of their hard conditions; and they esteemed his name, in contrast to the rest of the nation, who by their life-style despised God's name. God admires the faith of the humble and meek: he paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him of those who feared the Lord (3:16). His future response will make this plain, for in that day of the Lord he will honour the believing remnant – “they will be mine, says the Lord of hosts, on that day that I prepare my own possession, and I will spare them as a man spares his own son who serves him” (3:17). It is therefore not vain to serve the Lord: the Lord sees our service and remembers our labours, and though his reward may be delayed it will not be denied, whereas for the godless it will be denied, as Malachi 4:1-3 shows in the awful judgment awaiting those who have been superficial and not genuine God-fearers.
